claims.text: Equimolar WTaTiVZr has enhanced high-temperature plastic strain and toughness relative to commercially pure tungsten.
The enhanced plastic strain and toughness of WTaTiVZr are governed by a multiphase microstructure containing nanoscale precipitates and phase boundaries.
Repeated arc melting forms nanoscale precipitates and phase boundaries in WTaTiVZr.
The proposed multiphase microstructure facilitates dislocation mobility and grain-boundary sliding.
Repeated remelting ensures microstructural homogeneity in WTaTiVZr and pure tungsten.
The intrinsic multielement composition of WTaTiVZr produces nanoscale precipitates and phase boundaries during repeated melting.
Finely dispersed secondary-phase particles in WTaTiVZr relax dislocation pile-ups.
Finely dispersed secondary-phase particles in WTaTiVZr promote grain-boundary sliding.
Relaxation of dislocation pile-ups and promotion of grain-boundary sliding reduce local stress concentrations and delay crack initiation.
Reduced local stress concentrations and delayed crack initiation increase WTaTiVZr ductility and toughness relative to pure tungsten.
Pure tungsten has a single-phase microstructure.
Under high-temperature testing, WTaTiVZr will exhibit greater elongation and fracture toughness than pure tungsten.
Nanoscale precipitates will be present in WTaTiVZr but absent or significantly less prevalent in pure tungsten.
Commercially used pure tungsten has relatively low room-temperature ductility and high-temperature toughness.
The proposed mechanism is valid only while the nanoscale precipitates and phase boundaries remain stable at plasma-facing-component-relevant temperatures.
Prolonged service may cause additional phase transformations that limit the hypothesis's validity.
